title: Radioactive decay and half-life
objectives: Explain why decay is random for one nucleus but predictable for a large sample.
Define half-life, activity and the decay constant, and use λ = ln 2 / T½.
Use N = N₀(½)<sup>t/T½</sup> and N = N₀e<sup>−λt</sup>.
Read half-life from a decay curve and decay constant from a graph of ln N.

explanation.heading: Random, but predictable in bulk
body: Every unstable nucleus of a given isotope has the same fixed probability of decaying per second, called the decay constant λ. Nothing (not temperature, pressure or chemistry) changes it, and there is no way to say when a particular nucleus will go.
With millions of nuclei, though, the randomness averages out. The number decaying per second, the activity, is proportional to the number left: A = λN.

explanation.heading: Half-life
body: The half-life T½ is the time for the number of undecayed nuclei (or the activity) to halve. Crucially, it is the same however many nuclei you start with.
So after 3 half-lives, ⅛ remains. This is a geometric sequence with ratio ½.

explanation.heading: The exponential law
body: Because the rate of decay is proportional to N, dN/dt = −λN. The solution of that differential equation is
N = N₀ e−λt T½ = ln 2 / λ
Taking natural logs gives ln N = ln N₀ − λt, a straight line with gradient −λ. That is how λ is measured from data.

demo.intro: Each dot is a nucleus that decays at random. The plot compares what happens with the smooth exponential prediction.
notice: With a small sample the data is noticeably jagged; restart a few times and compare.
Each half-life, roughly half the remaining dots disappear, however many there were.
Switch to ln N: the prediction becomes a straight line of gradient −λ.

examples.title: Counting half-lives
examples.problem: A sample contains 8.0 × 10⁶ undecayed nuclei of an isotope with half-life 5.0 days. How many remain after 15 days?

steps.why: Whole numbers of half-lives can be done without logs.

examples.title: Using the decay constant
examples.problem: Carbon-14 has a half-life of 5730 years. What fraction of the original carbon-14 remains after 10 000 years?

steps.why: Keep λ in the same time unit as t.
A bit under a third, consistent with 10 000 y being a little under two half-lives.

examples.title: Half-life from activity
examples.problem: The activity of a sample falls from 800 Bq to 50 Bq in 12 hours. Find the half-life.

steps.why: Check whether the ratio is a power of 2.

takeaways: Decay is random and spontaneous, but N falls exponentially for a large sample.
Half-life is constant: it does not depend on how much you start with.
λ = ln 2 / T½, and ln N against t is a straight line of gradient −λ.
